heading: Welcome to MongArchive
text: MongArchive is an independent archive and research platform created to organize Mong history, records, language, identity, sources, maps, publications, and related materials in one place.

heading: Purpose
text: MongArchive was created to provide a clean and organized place for materials connected to Mong history, identity, language, records, books, articles, maps, oral histories, photographs, source notes, and related topics. The purpose is simple: help readers find materials more easily, keep important references organized, and support long term preservation through careful review, clear descriptions, and responsible presentation.

text: Browse organized collection pages for primary sources, historical records, maps, publications, language materials, media, and reviewed contributions.

heading: Submission Guidance
text: Learn how to send materials, source leads, corrections, records, oral histories, photographs, documents, and related information for review.

heading: How Materials Are Handled
text: Materials submitted to MongArchive are reviewed before they are added to public archive pages. Review may include checking relevance, source information, context, privacy, copyright concerns, and whether the material fits the archive. Review does not mean every claim is confirmed as final truth. It means materials are organized carefully, labeled when needed, and presented with enough context for readers to compare sources and think critically.

page: Scholar Taichiming Calls for United Nations Recognition of the Mong as an Indigenous People
heading: Calling for International Recognition
text: In his public message, Scholar Taichiming called for recognition of the Mong as an Indigenous people with their own name, history, identity, and cultural heritage. His request was not simply about changing a label. It was about protecting the Mong identity for future generations. For many years, Mong communities have faced confusion over names used by governments, scholars, missionaries, and outside institutions. Scholar Taichiming argued that the Mong people should have the right to identify themselves by their own traditional name.

page: Scholar Taichiming Calls for United Nations Recognition of the Mong as an Indigenous People
heading: A Request for Recognition
text: Scholar Taichiming’s public message should be understood as a request for recognition. It does not, by itself, mean that the United Nations has issued an official decision recognizing the Mong people. Official recognition would need to appear clearly in a United Nations report, recommendation, resolution, record, or other formal document. That written record is important because it could be studied, cited, shared, and preserved. It could also help researchers, educators, community leaders, and future generations explain who the Mong people are in an international setting.

page: Scholar Taichiming Calls for United Nations Recognition of the Mong as an Indigenous People
heading: Protecting the Mong Name
text: A major part of this effort is the protection of the name Mong. Names carry history. They connect people to their parents, grandparents, ancestors, homeland, language, and memory. When a people lose control of their name, they may also lose control of how others write about their past. Their identity may be placed under a larger government label or explained through terms they did not choose for themselves. page: Scholar Taichiming Calls for United Nations Recognition of the Mong as an Indigenous People
heading: Historical Background of the Mong People
text: The Mong people have deep historical roots in China and maintain a distinct language, identity, culture, and oral tradition. Over many generations, Mong communities also migrated into Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, Myanmar, and other parts of the world. Some Mong scholars and community historians connect the earliest Mong ancestors to ancient northern and central China, including areas near the Yellow River Basin and present day Shandong. These claims are important to Mong historical research, but the exact location and date of the earliest Mong origins remain subjects of continuing study and debate

page: Scholar Taichiming Calls for United Nations Recognition of the Mong as an Indigenous People
heading: Years of Research and Advocacy
text: Scholar Taichiming has spent years researching Mong history and sharing his findings with the public. He is the author of Mong China History and Heritage Preservation , a book focused on Mong history and cultural preservation. He has also served as president and executive director of Mong Heritage, an organization involved in Mong historical and cultural advocacy. His work has encouraged many Mong people to ask deeper questions: Who are we? What name did our ancestors use? How has our history been recorded? Who has the right to define our identity? The public appeal has brought the Mong recognition request before a wider international audience. The next steps will require careful research, historical documentation, community support, legal understanding, and continued communication with relevant United Nations bodies.
